entry.title: Digital that works, written down
entry.summary: A short manifesto I keep coming back to — and the three questions every build has to answer before a single pixel moves.
entry.content:
Every project I take on starts the same way: a long list of things the site could do, and a much shorter list of things it must do. The job is to get from the first list to the second without losing anything that matters.

the three questions

Before design, before code, I ask:

  1. Who is this for? Not “everyone”. One person, specifically.
  2. What should they do next? One action, measurable.
  3. What can we remove? Usually more than anyone expects.

Simple, fast, and engineered to drive measurable momentum. Everything else is decoration.

speed is a feature

Nobody notices a fast site, but everyone notices a slow one. I treat performance as a design constraint from day one, not something to fix at the end.

/* The whole palette. Four tones, one ink. */
:root {
  --ice:  #e3fdfd;
  --mist: #cbf1f5;
  --aqua: #a6e3e9;
  --teal: #71c9ce;
  --ink:  #17484d;
}
Budget Target Why
First paint < 1.0 s Feels instant on 4G
Total JS < 30 kB Less to parse, less to break
Fonts 1 file One variable woff2

what gets removed

The carousel. The second call to action. The “welcome to our website” paragraph. The animation that plays on every scroll.1

What’s left is usually a site that loads fast, says one thing clearly and asks for one thing politely. That’s the job.

  1. Motion is good when it explains something. Otherwise it’s a toll. ↩

entry.title: A grid you can see
entry.summary: Why I leave the column lines visible, and what they do for the reader.
entry.content:
Most grids hide. Mine stays on screen as a set of hairlines, because a visible structure makes the layout easy to read at a glance.

twelve columns, one rail

Content sits on a rail that spans ten of the twelve columns. The outer two act as margins and keep long lines from running wall to wall.

The desk where most of these layouts start: paper first.

lowercase, with a period

Headings are written in lowercase and end with a period. It reads like a statement rather than a sign.

entry.title: Notes from the studio
entry.summary: What making records teaches you about making websites.
entry.content:
A track and a homepage have more in common than you’d think. Both need a hook in the first few seconds, and both get worse when you add one more layer.

the mix is the edit

In the studio, most of the work is taking things out. The same goes for a layout: mute until it breaks, then bring back the last thing you muted.

entry.title: Along the coast
entry.summary: Working from the Costa del Sol, and why place still matters online.
entry.content:
Clients on the coast want to see that you know the coast. Local context shapes every brief: the languages, the seasons, the way people search.

work where your clients are

Being nearby still counts for something, even for work that ships online.

entry.title: What actually shipped this year?
entry.summary: A quick look back at what shipped, what stuck and what I'd delete.
entry.content:
Twelve months, a handful of launches and one lesson repeated in every project: ship the smallest useful version, then listen.

what stuck

Static sites, one font file, and forms that work without JavaScript.
